ABisector

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and watch its three angle bisectors meet in one spot.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press Check the claims to test what you see.
Look for the math

Every corner of a triangle has a line that cuts its angle exactly in half. The surprising part is that the three lines always meet at one point, and that point is the centre of a circle touching all three sides.

One line, two equal angles

An angle bisector is the line that splits an angle into two equal parts. In the picture, the two small arcs at each corner are coloured differently but have the same angle: angle(B,A,D) = angle(D,A,C), and the same at B and C. The logic test measures all three pairs on hundreds of triangles, including very obtuse ones, and the two halves agree every time.

Where the bisector cuts the far side

Let the bisector from A meet BC at D, and call the side lengths a = BC, b = CA, c = AB. Comparing the areas of triangles ABD and ACD in two ways gives the bisector theorem:

AB / AC = BD / DC  that is  c / b = BD / DC.

Both ways use the same altitude for one comparison and the same half-angle for the other, so everything cancels. The old archived page printed AB / BC in this line by mistake; the live article, and this page, give the correct AB / AC.

All three lines meet at one point

Apply the same ratio at the other two corners. The three ratios multiply to (c/b)(a/c)(b/a) = 1, which is exactly Ceva's theorem, so the three bisectors must pass through a single point. That point is the incenter. It is equally far from all three sides, so it is the centre of the incircle drawn here.

Drag one of the small dots along a bisector toward the centre: its circle touches one side, and at the incenter it just touches all three.

Side lengths as weights

There is a short way to find both points. Put weights a, b, c at the corners A, B, C. Their balance point is the incenter, and leaving out one weight gives the foot on the opposite side: D = (b·B + c·C)/(b+c). The radius is r = area / s, where s = (a+b+c)/2. The logic test checks these formulas against the applet's own construction — rotate a ray by half the angle and intersect two lines — on hundreds of triangles.

Try making a very long, thin, obtuse triangle: the three lines still meet, and the circle still fits inside.
